title: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a primary phenomenon.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I, for my part, see no subtle mystery in the matter, other than what lies in the steady production of similar growing parts, similarly situated, at similar successive intervals of time.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIV, “On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis”; topic “Church's theory of phyllotaxis”. Scope: phyllotaxis of leaves, florets, bracts and scales

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch14-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A predictive developmental model can test a restricted sufficiency claim. Thompson's broad language is partly circular and existing time-lapse data have narrow taxonomic coverage.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use time-lapse meristem datasets to quantify initiation intervals, organ similarity and placement, then test whether these inputs alone predict subsequent helical or spiral arrangements. Accurate out-of-sample prediction supports sufficiency; systematic need for additional interactions refutes the 'necessarily' claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Mechanical and inhibitory interactions are plausible hidden variables.

Time-resolved organ initiation datasets cover few species.

'Similarly placed' risks defining the resulting pattern circularly.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Regular spacing of similar parts does generate helices on a cylinder and logarithmic spirals on a surface that includes the pole, and existing capitulum counts can illustrate that geometry. The same patterns are the output of later physiological models, so a successful geometric reconstruction does not discriminate Thompson's deflationary account from those rivals. The lattice prediction is testable; the claim that there is nothing further to explain is not decided by the fit.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: From primordia positions and plastochron, simulate the lattice produced by similar organs placed at equal intervals and compare it with observed helices and spirals. Agreement shows that regular production is sufficient to generate the pattern; it does not show that no further physiological process is involved, because auxin transport and mechanical buckling act by creating that regularity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Any mechanism that spaces organs evenly will satisfy the mathematical consequence Thompson treats as the whole explanation.

The denial of a 'further mystery' does not specify an observation that developmental models cannot also match.
